payload.name: observer-controller
payload.scope: To implement state-space control when not all states are directly measurable, by combining a state estimator with a state-feedback law into a single dynamic compensator.

definition.body: observer-controller is a human-authored control design methodology that combines a state observer with a state-feedback controller, using the observer's estimated states as inputs to the feedback law so that a complete control system can be built when not all states are directly measurable. Parameters: (1) an observer (typically Luenberger or Kalman) that estimates the state vector from available measurements; (2) a feedback gain law (e.g. u = -Kx_hat) that drives the estimated states toward desired values; (3) the combined dynamics where the observer and controller eigenvalues are distinct and the control law acts on estimated rather than true states. It persists as the standard implementation pattern for state-space control in practice — whenever full state measurement is unavailable, the observer-controller architecture is the canonical solution — encoded in control engineering texts (Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; Chen, Linear System Theory), embedded in MATLAB's ctrlsynth toolchains, and deployed in aerospace, robotics, and process control systems. e.g.: Luenberger-based observer-controller for a DC-motor speed loop where only encoder feedback is available; Kalman-filter-based observer-controller for satellite attitude control using star tracker measurements; embedded observer-controller on a quadcopter flight controller using IMU measurements | not: full-state feedback (uses actual states directly, no observer); output-feedback (uses a static gain on outputs, not a dynamic observer) [formal: controlator observatorque | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: mu-synthesis
payload.scope: To design controllers that ensure robust performance against structured uncertainty by minimizing the structured singular value (mu) of the closed-loop system.

definition.body: mu-synthesis is a human-authored robust control design methodology that iteratively designs a controller to minimize the structured singular value (mu) of the closed-loop system across frequency, ensuring robust stability and performance against structured plant uncertainty. Parameters: (1) a generalized plant model with structured uncertainty blocks (delta) representing parametric variations and unmodeled dynamics; (2) D-K iteration: alternating between scaling matrices D (for mu minimization) and K-controller synthesis (H-infinity optimization for each iteration); (3) the structured singular value mu which quantifies the worst-case effect of the uncertainty structure on closed-loop performance. It persists as the premier method for robust control design with structured uncertainty in aerospace and high-performance systems, documented in canonical texts (Doyle, 'History of Robust Control'; Zhou, Doyle and Glover, 'Robust and Optimal Control'; Balakrishnan and Doyle) and implemented in MATLAB's mu synthesis and DK-synthesis toolboxes. e.g.: D-K iteration for a hypersonic vehicle flight control system with 20% thrust uncertainty blocks; mu-synthesized autopilot for an F-16 across a grid of flight conditions; robust guidance law for a reusable launch vehicle with mass and inertia uncertainties | not: H-infinity control (minimizes worst-case gain for unstructured uncertainty, not structured singular value); LMI-based robust control (convex optimization approach, not D-K iteration) [formal: synthetica valoris structurate singularis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: structured-singular-value
payload.scope: To quantify the worst-case effect of structured plant uncertainty on closed-loop stability and performance, generalizing the singular value to account for specific uncertainty patterns.

definition.body: structured-singular-value is a human-authored mathematical measure that quantifies the worst-case effect of structured matrix uncertainty on closed-loop stability. It is defined as mu_M(N) = 1 / min(sigma_delta) over all complex structured perturbations delta in the set M with sigma_max(delta) <= 1, where N is the nominal matrix and M is the structured uncertainty set. When mu_M(N) > 1, there exists a structured perturbation causing instability; when mu_M(N) <= 1, the system is robustly stable for all allowed uncertainties. It persists as the central robustness metric in mu-synthesis and structured uncertainty analysis, encoded in mathematical control theory (Doyle, 'Structured Uncertainty in Control Systems'; Zhou, Doyle and Glover), implemented in MATLAB's musyn and mu analysis tools, and used in aerospace robust flight control certification. e.g.: computing mu for a flexible spacecraft with 6 structured inertia uncertainties at 10 Hz; mu analysis of an H-II thrust vector control system with actuator uncertainty blocks; structured singular value of a flight controller evaluated across a frequency grid from 0.1 to 100 Hz | not: singular-value (the unstructured matrix measure sigma_max, which does not account for uncertainty structure); H-infinity norm (worst-case gain over all unit-norm perturbations, not structured ones) [formal: valor singularis structurate | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: loop-shaping
payload.scope: To shape the loop gain frequency response across bandwidth so that closed-loop systems meet robustness and performance specifications through frequency-domain design.

definition.body: Loop-shaping is a human-authored frequency-domain control design methodology that shapes the loop gain magnitude and phase response across frequency to achieve desired closed-loop performance and robustness specifications. The construct maps the trade-off between sensitivity attenuation at low frequencies, disturbance rejection at mid-frequencies, and noise sensitivity at high frequencies, parameterized by crossover frequency, bandwidth, and roll-off rate. The persistence mechanism: maintained as a core design procedure in classical and modern control (Skogestad and Postlethwaite; Zhou, Doyle, and Glover), taught in all control engineering curricula, and implemented in MATLAB loop-shaping design tools and mu-synthesis workflows. It is distinct from pole-placement (time-domain eigenvalue assignment, not frequency shaping) and from LQR (optimal quadratic design, not heuristic frequency shaping). e.g.: shaping loop gain for an aircraft pitch channel to achieve 30 deg phase margin and 10 rad/s crossover; loop-shaping of a DC-DC converter to reject 100 Hz line ripple while limiting high-frequency noise gain; hard-disk-drive servo loop shaped to reject mechanical resonances above 1 kHz | not: pole-placement (time-domain eigenvalue assignment, not frequency-domain shaping); LQR (optimal quadratic cost minimization, not heuristic frequency shaping); root-locus (analytical method for visualizing pole migration with scalar gain variation, not a synthesis procedure) [formal: modelatio loopae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lmi
payload.scope: A convex constraint in robust control and optimization where a symmetric matrix, linear in decision variables, must be positive or negative semidefinite. Serves as the unifying computational framework for H-infinity control, pole placement, and robust stability analysis, replacing non-convex Riccati equations with tractable convex feasibility problems. Persisted in YALMPI, SeDuMi, Mosek, and SDPT4 solvers.

definition.body: A linear matrix inequality (LMI) is a convex constraint of the form F(x) = F₀ + x₁F₁ + ⋯ + xₙFₙ ≽ 0, where F₀, F₁, …, Fₙ are symmetric matrices of fixed dimension, x = (x₁, …, xₙ) are real decision variables, and ≽ 0 denotes positive semidefiniteness. The feasible set is the intersection of an affine subspace with the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, making LMI feasibility solvable in polynomial time via interior-point methods. Parameters: (1) the number of decision variables n, (2) the matrix dimension p×p, (3) the matrix coefficients F₀ through Fₙ. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: LMI problems are encoded in convex optimization software (YALMPI, CVX, MOSEK) and solved as semidefinite programs (SDPs) across control synthesis, structural design, and operations research. e.g.: MATLAB's Robust Control Toolbox lmivar; YALMPI LMI model for H-infinity synthesis; CVX semidefinite program for robust state-feedback gain; SeDuMi solver for mixed sensitivity LMI | not: SDP; Lyapunov equation; scalar linear inequality [formal: inaequalitas matricialis linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: youla-parametrization
payload.scope: A mathematical construction in robust control that parameterizes the set of all stabilizing controllers for a linear plant using a stable free parameter Q. Enables systematic synthesis of optimal controllers via convex optimization over the Youla parameter. Persisted in control theory textbooks and robust control software toolboxes.

definition.body: A Youla parametrization is a mathematical construction that parameterizes the set of all stabilizing controllers for a given linear time-invariant plant P. Given a plant P and a doubly coprime factorization P = NM⁻¹ = Ĩ⁻¹Ñ, every stabilizing controller C is expressed as C = (X + QD̃)(Ñ + MQ)⁻¹ where Q is an arbitrary stable transfer function (the Youla parameter), and X, D̃, Ñ, M are fixed stable factors from the coprime factorization. Parameters: (1) the plant P, (2) the doubly coprime factorization (N,M,Ñ,D̃), (3) the baseline stabilizing controller X. The parametrization persists through control theory textbooks and robust control software, where Q is optimized to meet performance and robustness specifications. e.g.: MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox youla function; Zhou-Doyle-Glover textbook parametrization; Python control library coprime factorization; Vidyasagar's Youla parametrization in H-infinity design | not: doubly coprime factorization; state-feedback; PID controller [formal: parametrizatio youla | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Parameters: (1) the plant P, (2) the doubly coprime factorization (N,M,Ñ,D̃), (3) the baseline stabilizing controller X. The parametrization persists through control theory textbooks and robust control software, where Q is optimized to meet performance and robustness specifications. e.g.: MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox youla function; Zhou-Doyle-Glover textbook parametrization; Python control library coprime factorization; Vidyasagar's Youla parametrization in H-infinity design | not: doubly coprime factorization; state-feedback; PID controller [formal: parametrizatio youla | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: h-infinity-control
payload.scope: A robust control design methodology that synthesizes a controller to minimize the worst-case gain of the closed-loop system from disturbances to controlled outputs. Uses state-space methods to achieve guaranteed performance and stability margins. Persisted in aerospace guidance, robotics, and process control toolboxes.

definition.body: H-infinity control is a robust control design methodology that synthesizes a controller K to minimize the H-infinity norm (worst-case gain across all frequencies) of the weighted closed-loop transfer function from disturbances to controlled outputs. The method formulates a generalized plant P(s) with performance weights, uncertainty weights, and actuator weights, then computes K to minimize ||F_l(P,K)||_inf < gamma. Parameters: (1) the generalized plant P(s) structure, (2) performance weighting functions, (3) the H-infinity norm bound gamma, (4) the state-space dimension of the controller. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in robust control software and textbook pedagogy. e.g.: MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox hinfnorm for aerospace flight controller; Zhou-Doyle-Glover textbook H-infinity synthesis for robotic manipulator; Skogestad H-infinity design for chemical process control; Anderson-Moore H-infinity optimal control for satellite attitude | not: H-infinity norm; LQR; mu-synthesis [formal: infini norm control | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: doubly-coprime-factorization

definition.body: A doubly coprime factorization of a linear plant P(s) expresses P(s) as P = NM⁻¹ = D̃⁻¹Ñ where N, M, Ñ, D̃ are stable proper transfer function matrices satisfying the Bézout identity: NX + MY = ÑX̃ + ỸM = I for stable X,Y,X̃,Ỹ. Computed from plant state-space (A,B,C,D) via two Riccati equations. Parameters: (1) the plant P(s), (2) the stable factors N,M,Ñ,D̃, (3) the Bézout identity matrices X,Y,X̃,Ỹ. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: computed by robust control software (MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox tf2dcmr) and textbook algorithms (Zhou-Doyle-Glover). e.g.: MATLAB tf2dcmr for H-infinity design; Zhou-Doyle-Glover Chapter 6 DCMF algorithm; Skogestad course notes on DCMF; Vidyasagar textbook DCMF for robust synthesis | not: coprime factorization; state-space model; Youla parametrization [formal: factorizatio coprima gemina | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lead-lag-compensator
payload.scope: To simultaneously improve a feedback system transient response and steady-state accuracy using a single compensator network with both phase-lead and phase-lag sections, parameterized by crossover frequency, phase-lag center frequency, and attenuation factors for each section.

definition.body: Lead-lag compensator is a human-made controller transfer function that combines a phase-lead section and a phase-lag section into a single compensator, enabling simultaneous improvement of transient response (via phase lead near crossover) and steady-state accuracy (via low-frequency gain boost from phase lag). Its standard form is C(s) = K(s/z_lead + 1)/(s/p_lead + 1) * (s/z_lag + 1)/(s/p_lag + 1) where p_lead > z_lead (phase-lead section) and p_lag < z_lag (phase-lag section). The lead section zero and pole are centered near the crossover frequency to add phase margin; the lag section zero and pole are centered well below crossover to boost low-frequency gain without significantly degrading phase margin. Parameters: (1) lead zero and pole locations setting phase-lead frequency and magnitude, (2) lag zero and pole locations setting phase-lag frequency and attenuation, (3) overall gain K. It is distinct from lead-compensator (phase lead only, no low-frequency gain boost), lag-compensator (low-frequency gain boost only, no phase lead), and PID-controller (different structure and tuning objectives). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a standard compensator design in classical control engineering — implemented in analog lead-lag networks, digital compensator sections, and tuning procedures in frequency-response design — encoded in Ogata Modern Control Engineering, Dorf and Smith Modern Control Engineering, and process control design practice. e.g.: lead-lag for DC motor speed control with 20 deg phase margin improvement; lead-lag compensator in aircraft pitch channel for transient and steady-state performance; compensator for DC-DC converter with lead at 1 kHz and lag at 100 Hz | not: lead-compensator (phase lead only, no lag section for low-frequency gain); lag-compensator (low-frequency gain boost only, no phase lead); cascaded lead-lag as two separate compensators in series, not a single network [formal: compensans principalis-retardans compositus | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.note: DEPENDS_ON test: LMI is developed as a framework to replace Riccati equations in control synthesis. The scope states LMI serves to 'replace non-convex Riccati equations with tractable convex feasibility problems.' The Riccati equation is the foundational nonlinear matrix equation whose solution yields optimal gains; LMI generalizes this by reformulating the synthesis as a convex feasibility problem over matrix inequalities. The removal test: removing the Riccati equation concept removes the mathematical foundation that LMI generalizes and replaces — LMI as a control synthesis framework only exists as an alternative to Riccati-based methods. Without the Riccati equation concept, LMI loses its motivation and target, becoming just a general convex constraint with no control-theoretic anchoring.

payload.name: h-infinity-control
payload.scope: To design controllers for plants whose exact dynamics are unknown within a norm-bounded set, guaranteeing performance and stability against the worst admissible plant rather than the nominal one, where a single mean-square optimum (LQR) cannot certify robustness.

definition.body: H-infinity control is a design methodology that control engineering drew around the problem of designing a controller for a plant whose exact dynamics are unknown within a norm-bounded set, so that performance and robustness are certified against the worst admissible plant rather than the nominal one. The line it draws: it takes in the design problems whose specification is a bound on the worst-case gain — the H-infinity norm of a closed-loop transfer function from disturbance inputs to error outputs — under additive or multiplicative plant uncertainty, with the design criterion the minimization of that bound; it leaves out nominal optimal design (LQR minimizes a mean-square cost of a known plant and carries no uncertainty bound), classical margin-based loop shaping (Bode design by gain and phase margins, with no norm minimization), and the mu refinement (mu-synthesis, which adds D-scaling for structured uncertainty and stands as a separate construct). Parameters: (1) the plant uncertainty class — additive or multiplicative, with its norm bound; (2) the performance channels — which weighted disturbance-to-error transfer function is to be bounded; (3) the synthesis route — the Bounded Real Lemma recast as a pair of Riccati equations, or as linear matrix inequalities for multi-objective specifications; (4) the design criterion — the least achievable H-infinity norm gamma. Its operation: the controller produced is the robust counterpart of the LQR gain, obtained at the smallest gamma for which the Bounded Real condition holds. It persists as the standard robust design procedure of the discipline: named H-infinity in the robust control literature since the 1980s, taught as the core synthesis procedure in Zhou, Doyle, and Glover, Robust and Optimal Control (1989), and in Skogestad and Postlethwaite, Multivariable Feedback Control, computed by MATLAB's hinfrfn and the Robust Control Toolbox, and applied in disk-drive servo, active vibration isolation, and aerospace control design. e.g.: H-infinity synthesis of a CD disk-drive head-positioning servo (documented robust control application); H-infinity controller design for an active vibration isolation mount (documented application in machine control); MATLAB hinfrfn computing the optimal gain for a nominal plant under multiplicative uncertainty; the H-infinity synthesis examples worked in Zhou, Doyle, and Glover, Robust and Optimal Control (1989) | not: LQR gain design (mean-square cost of a nominal plant, no worst-case bound); Bode loop-shaping by gain and phase margins (classical design, no norm minimization); mu-synthesis with D-scaling (the structured-uncertainty refinement, a separate construct) [formal: regulatio normae infinitae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phase-vocoder-stretch
payload.scope: A human-made audio signal processing technique for time-scale modification using the phase vocoder architecture.

definition.body: Phase-vocoder-stretch is a specific application of the phase vocoder that changes the perceived duration of audio while preserving pitch. It operates by computing the short-time Fourier transform of the input, resampling the magnitude spectrum along the time axis, and adjusting phase relationships between consecutive frames to maintain coherence, then reconstructing via inverse STFT and overlap-add. It is distinguished from generic phase vocoder by its time-stretching intent and the specific resampling of the magnitude axis, not pitch shifting. It persists through software implementations in audio editing tools, DAWs, and research libraries. e.g.: Rubber Band Library time-stretch; Paulstretch (Paulstretch software); SoundTouch library; Audacity Change Tempo; Adobe Audition Stretch tool | not: phase-vocoder-pitch-shift; time-stretching via granular synthesis; spectral freeze [formal: extensio vocator phaseum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: extended-kalman-filter
payload.scope: A nonlinear state estimation algorithm that linearizes the system's nonlinear state-transition and observation models around the current estimate using Jacobian matrices, extending the linear Kalman filter to handle smooth nonlinear dynamics.

definition.body: The extended Kalman filter is a nonlinear state estimation algorithm that extends the linear Kalman filter by linearizing the system's nonlinear state-transition and observation models around the current state estimate using Jacobian matrices. At each step it (1) propagates the state through the nonlinear function f evaluated at the current estimate, (2) computes the Jacobian of f with respect to the state to form the linearized state-transition matrix, (3) propagates the error covariance through the linearized matrix, and (4) fuses the measurement through the linearized observation model h evaluated at the predicted state, computing its Jacobian for the linearized gain. Its parameters are the nonlinear state-transition function f, the observation function h, the process and measurement noise covariances, and the initial state estimate. It persists as the standard nonlinear estimation method in navigation, robotics, and tracking systems where the nonlinearity is smooth and the Jacobian is computable. e.g.: EKF-based GPS/INS navigation fusion in the Navstar GPS standard; robot localization using the ROSS EKF implementation; aircraft state estimation in the Honeywell EKF-based inertial navigation system | not: unscented Kalman filter (uses sigma-point propagation instead of Jacobian linearization); particle filter (uses sequential Monte Carlo instead of Gaussian approximation) [formal: filtrum extendum kalmanii | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: unscented-kalman-filter
payload.scope: A nonlinear state estimation algorithm that propagates mean and covariance through a deterministic set of sigma points sampled from the posterior, avoiding Jacobian computation and capturing nonlinearities to at least second-order accuracy.

definition.body: The unscented Kalman filter is a nonlinear state estimation algorithm that avoids Jacobian linearization by using a deterministic set of sigma points to capture the distribution of the state. At each step it (1) generates 2n+1 sigma points from the current mean and covariance, where n is the state dimension, (2) propagates each sigma point through the nonlinear state-transition function f, (3) recomputes the mean and covariance of the transformed points including process noise, (4) generates sigma points from the predicted distribution, (5) propagates them through the observation function h, and (6) fuses the measurement using the computed cross-covariance to update the estimate. Its parameters are the nonlinear state-transition function f, the observation function h, the process and measurement noise covariances, the weighting parameters lambda, alpha, and beta for sigma-point generation, and the initial state estimate. It persists as the preferred nonlinear estimation method in systems where the Jacobian is expensive or inaccurate to compute, widely implemented in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and attitude estimation. e.g.: Sigma-point filter in the UKF MATLAB Toolbox by Julier and Uhlmann; attitude estimation using the QTUKF algorithm in aerospace GNSS/INS integration; 6-DOF spacecraft orbit determination using the UKF in the NASA JPL guidance and navigation software | not: extended Kalman filter (linearizes via Jacobian matrices instead of sigma-point propagation); particle filter (uses random sampling and weights instead of deterministic sigma points) [formal: filtrum umbrae caeruleae kalmanii | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The particle filter is a sequential Monte Carlo state estimation algorithm that represents the posterior distribution of the state as a set of weighted samples (particles). At each step it (1) propagates each particle through the nonlinear state-transition function with added process noise samples, (2) reweights particles based on how well their predicted measurements match the actual observation using the measurement likelihood, and (3) resamples to eliminate particles with low weights and replicate high-weight particles, mitigating degeneracy. Its parameters are the nonlinear state-transition function f, the observation function h, the process noise distribution, the measurement noise distribution, the initial particle set, the number of particles N, and the resampling strategy. It persists as the standard approach for nonlinear, non-Gaussian estimation in tracking, localization, and robotics where the posterior is multimodal or the system is too nonlinear for Gaussian approximations. e.g.: Monte Carlo localization in the KTH Robotics lab's Monte Carlo Localization library; target tracking using the ISAC particle filter in the IEEE Radar Conference benchmark; visual odometry in the ORB-SLAM3 particle filter-based tracking module | not: Kalman filter (assumes Gaussian posterior, uses analytical propagation); ensemble Kalman filter (propagates ensemble through dynamics with Gaussian sampling, not importance-weighted resampling) [formal: filtrum particulare | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bounded-real-lemma
payload.scope: The theorem of robust control made to turn an H-infinity norm bound on a closed-loop transfer function into an algebraic test - a matrix inequality or a Riccati solvability condition - so that H-infinity synthesis can be computed by state-space or LMI methods instead of pointwise frequency checking.

definition.body: The bounded real lemma (BRL) is a theorem of robust and optimal control giving an exact equivalence for a stable, or stabilizable-and-detectable, system G with state-space realization (A,B,C,D): (i) the H-infinity norm of G is strictly less than a given gamma, i.e. the supremum of the complex magnitude of G over all real frequencies is below gamma; (ii) a Hermitian matrix P exists satisfying the associated bounded-real (KYP) matrix inequality, a linear matrix inequality in P built from (A,B,C,D) and gamma; and (iii) the associated algebraic Riccati equation has a unique stabilizing solution P. Parameters: (1) the transfer function G or its realization (A,B,C,D); (2) the bound gamma > 0. It persists as the bridge of H-infinity design: the named step converting the frequency-domain requirement into (a) the dual-Riccati route of H-infinity synthesis as implemented in MATLAB's hinfsyn and (b) the LMI route solvable by interior-point semidefinite programming, and it is taught as a named theorem in the robust-control texts. e.g.: the bounded-real equivalence in Zhou-Doyle-Glover Robust and Optimal Control (1996); the bounded-real matrix condition in the H-infinity chapter of Skogestad and Postlethwaite (2005); the Riccati-based step of MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox hinfsyn | not: the small-gain theorem (stability of a loop product, not a norm-bound equivalence); the H-infinity norm (the quantity the lemma bounds, not the equivalence) [formal: lemma limitatae realitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: kalman-yakubovich-popov-lemma
payload.scope: A theorem of linear systems theory made to provide a computable test for positive-realness of transfer functions via linear matrix inequalities, enabling passivity-based and robust control synthesis.

definition.body: The Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov lemma is a theorem of linear systems theory giving an exact equivalence between the frequency-domain positive-realness condition of a transfer function and the existence of a solution to a linear matrix inequality (the KYP inequality) involving the system's state-space matrices. Specifically, a strictly proper transfer function G(s)=C(sI-A)^-1B is positive-real (Re[G(jw)] >= 0 for all real w) if and only if there exists a symmetric matrix P >= 0 such that A^T P + P A <= 0, C = B^T P, and the pair (A,C) is observable. Parameters: (1) the state-space realization (A,B,C,D); (2) the frequency bound omega; (3) the LMI variable P and slack variables. The persistence mechanism is theoretical: proven in control theory literature, taught as a named theorem in graduate-level systems theory, and applied in passivity-based control design, adaptive control, and robust control synthesis. e.g.: the KYP lemma in Zhou-Doyle-Glover Robust and Optimal Control (1996) Chapter 4; the KYP lemma in Willems' dissipativity theory; MATLAB's Robust Control Toolbox positive_real check; the KYP lemma in Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy control synthesis via LMIs | not: the bounded real lemma (bounds H-infinity norm rather than positive-realness, different matrix inequality); the positive-real lemma (alternate name for KYP; this entry covers both) [formal: lemma Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: small-gain-theorem
payload.scope: A theorem of robust control made to provide a simple sufficient condition for the stability of feedback interconnections based on the product of the gains of the two subsystems.

definition.body: The small-gain theorem is a theorem of robust control stating that a feedback interconnection of two stable systems is stable if the product of their H-infinity gains is strictly less than one. Formally, if G1 and G2 are causal operators with finite L2-induced gains ||G1|| and ||G2||, and ||G1|| * ||G2|| < 1, then the feedback interconnection is input-output stable. Parameters: (1) the two subsystems G1 and G2; (2) their L2-induced gains ||G1|| and ||G2||; (3) the gain product bound gamma < 1. The persistence mechanism is theoretical: proven in systems theory and robust control literature, taught as a fundamental stability result in graduate-level control courses, and applied in robust control synthesis, adaptive control, and nonlinear system analysis. e.g.: the small-gain theorem in Zhou-Doyle-Glover Robust and Optimal Control (1996) Chapter 3; the small-gain theorem in Vidyasagar's Nonlinear Systems Analysis (2002); the small-gain condition in MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox systune; the small-gain theorem in integral input-to-state stability literature | not: the bounded real lemma (H-infinity norm equivalence, not a feedback stability result); the circle criterion (nonlinear feedback stability, not gain-product based) [formal: theorema parvi productus | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: passivity
payload.scope: A property of dynamical systems made to characterize energy dissipation and storage, enabling stability analysis of feedback interconnections through energy-based arguments.

definition.body: Passivity is a property of a dynamical system stating that the system cannot generate energy internally — the total energy supplied to the system over any time interval is at least as large as the increase in stored energy. Formally, a causal system S with input u and output y is passive if there exists a scalar alpha such that integral from 0 to T of y(t)^T u(t) dt >= -alpha for all T >= 0. A system is strictly passive if the inequality is strict. Parameters: (1) the input-output pair (u, y); (2) the storage function V(x) representing stored energy; (3) the supply rate w(u, y) quantifying energy flow. The persistence mechanism is theoretical: proven in control theory literature, taught as a fundamental stability concept in graduate-level courses, and applied in robotics (impedance control), networked systems, and robust control synthesis. e.g.: passivity in Willems' Dissipative Systems Theory (1972); passivity-based control in Ortega, van der Schaft, Mareels, and Maschke's Putting Passivity (2001); MATLAB's passivity analysis tools in Robust Control Toolbox; passivity in adaptive control of Euler-Lagrange systems | not: passive network (a circuit composed of passive elements — this entry covers the general dynamical systems property); positive-real function (a transfer function property related by the KYP lemma, not passivity itself) [formal: passivitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
